wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
wine.classification: Grand Cru, one of the seven climats of the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Parcels of Les Clos, the largest of the seven grand cru climats, on the hill that faces south west across the Serein from the town; stony limestone high on the slope, deeper clay lower down.
wine.making: Fermented in tank, then moved to old oak casks, among them the traditional Chablis feuillette of about 132 litres, with little or no new wood. The wine rests on its fine lees for a year or more before it is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Oyster shell, lemon pith and green apple over wet chalk, with a note of iodine; tight and dense, with high acidity and a long, saline finish that turns towards honey, hazelnut and dried mushroom with age.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first five to ten years, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass with a wide bowl.

label.means: The one appellation for the seven climats on the hill across the Serein from the town.
The climat, the largest of the seven, its name recalling the dry stone walls that once enclosed it.
The founder's name, which the domaine's labels carry.

records.table: From the largest of the seven Chablis grand cru climats, Raveneau's Les Clos is fermented in tank and raised in old casks with little or no new wood. Tight and saline when young, it needs years in bottle, so decant it and pour it cool rather than cold.
records.story: Chablis grew rich in the Middle Ages on wine shipped down the Yonne to Paris, and the story goes that Les Clos was among the first slopes worked by the Cistercian monks of Pontigny, an abbey founded in 1114; its name recalls the dry stone walls that once enclosed the vines. Frost, phylloxera and war shrank the vineyard, and in 1938 the law gave the hill's seven climats a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. Ten years later François Raveneau, who died in 2000, married into the Dauvissat family and joined his vines to theirs. Earlier generations had sold their grapes; he was the first of the family to bottle wine under its own name. Through the 1960s and 1970s, as grand cru land came up for sale, he bought parcels in Les Clos, Valmur and Blanchot. His two sons worked beside him for years before they took charge, and they kept his method: fermentation in tank, then a year and more in old casks. In their cellar Les Clos shows that Chablis can be raised in wood and keep the taste of its limestone. On a list it belongs with the wines to cellar, not with the crisp aperitifs.

others.name: Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre
others.note: The premier cru that adjoins the grand cru hill, raised in old casks like the grands crus.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Valmur
others.note: The broadest of the domaine's grands crus, from the climat between Grenouilles and Les Clos.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Blanchot
others.note: From the climat at the south eastern end of the hill, beside Les Clos.

traps: Chablis Grand Cru is one appellation of seven climats on a single hill, not seven appellations or seven villages.
Raveneau is Chablis raised in old wood: call it neither steel fresh nor new oaked, since the casks give texture and no taste of oak.
Domaine Raveneau and Domaine Vincent Dauvissat are linked by marriage but are separate estates.

cards.front: Raveneau Les Clos: in what is it fermented, and in what is it then raised?
cards.back: Fermented in tank, then raised for a year and more in old oak casks, the Chablis feuillette among them.

cards.front: When was Domaine Raveneau founded, and how did its first vines come together?
cards.back: In 1948, when François Raveneau married into the Dauvissat family and joined his vines to theirs.

questions.q: A guest ordering Raveneau's Les Clos asks how it differs from the other Chablis grand cru climats. Which fact fits?
opts: It is the largest of the seven, facing south west
It is the smallest of the seven, between Vaudésir and Valmur
It is a premier cru that adjoins the grand cru hill
It is a walled monopole on the left bank of the Serein
questions.exp: Les Clos is the largest of the seven climats, on the south west facing hill above the Serein; Grenouilles is the smallest, and Montée de Tonnerre is the premier cru beside the hill.

questions.q: Domaine Raveneau began in 1948 with family vines. How did it come to hold Les Clos, Valmur and Blanchot?
opts: Its founder bought parcels in the 1960s and 1970s
The monks of Pontigny left them to the family
The Chablis cooperative passed them on in 1923
The appellation decree of 1938 granted them
questions.exp: François Raveneau bought grand cru parcels in the 1960s and 1970s, as land came up for sale; 1923 is the cooperative's founding, and the decree of 1938 drew the appellation, not anyone's holdings.

report: The library's style line says the wines are fermented and aged partly in old barrels; the Wikipedia account and the Decanter profile both say fermentation is in tank and the wine goes to cask after it, so the record says tank, then old casks.
François Raveneau's year of birth was not found in any source read; he is named once, with the year of his death, 2000, which three accounts give.
The year he stepped back is 1988 in one account and 1995 in another, so the story says only that his sons worked beside him for years before they took charge; both sons are living and are not named.
The arrival of the wines in the United States in the early 1980s rests on one account and is left out, as are the sizes of the parcels, which are volatile.
The size of Les Clos, its aspect and soils and the origin of its name are the Chablis wine body's own pages; the Pontigny origin is that body's hedged may be, told here as a story.
One account says the domaine has moved towards larger casks since a new cellar of 2013; with no second source the record keeps to old casks and the feuillette.

changed: making, table and story: the claim of no new wood at all is now little or no new wood, or left out, since accounts differ on whether the domaine buys a few new barrels each year; the library says only old barrels.
cards[0]: the card asked how much new oak and answered none at all; it now asks where the wine is fermented and where it is raised, which every account agrees on: tank, then old casks.
open: François Raveneau is named with the year of his death, 2000, alone: his year of birth was found in no source, so the integrator may prefer to call him the founder.
The purchases of grand cru parcels through the 1960s and 1970s rest on the author's searched secondary sources; the refuter could open no page to confirm the decades.

wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Preuses
wine.classification: Grand Cru, one of the seven climats of the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Les Preuses, towards the north western end of the grand cru hill between Bougros and Vaudésir, on the Kimmeridgian limestone and marl of the right bank of the Serein; the vines are farmed organically.
wine.making: Raised in oak, chiefly in old barrels and the traditional Chablis feuillette, with only a little new wood, and left long on its lees, so the cask shapes the texture without giving any taste of oak. It is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Lemon rind, crushed shell and white peach over chalk, rounder and more open than the house's Les Clos, with a quiet, creamy texture, bright acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: More giving young than the house's Les Clos, it rewards ten years in bottle and keeps well beyond that in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly and an old one not at all; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: One appellation shared by the seven climats on the hill across the Serein from the town.
The climat, between Bougros and Vaudésir towards the north western end of the hill.
The name many labels carry, for the founder's son and grandson; the domaine is also known by the grandson's name alone.

records.table: Dauvissat's Les Preuses is a Chablis grand cru from the north western reach of the hill, raised in old casks and feuillettes with barely any new wood. It is rounder and more open than the house's Les Clos, yet stony and saline, and it rewards ten years in bottle.
records.story: Bottling at the domaine was rare in Chablis in 1931, when most growers sold their wine in cask to the merchants, but that year the founder of this estate, built up through the 1920s, began to bottle his own. In 1938 Chablis Grand Cru became an appellation, and the seven climats of the hill took one name on the label with their own beneath it. The founder's son widened the holdings from the 1950s, and the family became kin by marriage to the Raveneaus, so the two domaines that would be named together grew up side by side. The founder's grandson joined in the 1970s and took charge in 1989. He kept the cellar as he found it: old barrels, the small Chablis feuillette, long lees ageing and no taste of new oak, and in the early 2000s he turned the vineyards to organic farming. Les Preuses and Les Clos are the domaine's two grands crus, the first rounder and more open, the second firmer and slower. When a guest asks for Chablis raised in wood that keeps the taste of its limestone, Dauvissat is the other name beside Raveneau, and Les Preuses is the easier of its grands crus to open young.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
others.note: The domaine's other grand cru, firmer and slower to open than Les Preuses.

others.name: Chablis Premier Cru La Forest
others.note: The premier cru that is the house's calling card, spelled La Forest without an accent.

traps: Domaine Vincent Dauvissat is distinct from the other Dauvissat estates of Chablis, so read the first name on the label.
La Forest is spelled without an accent and is a premier cru, not a grand cru.
Les Preuses is a grand cru climat; Montée de Tonnerre and La Forest, often poured beside it, are premiers crus.

cards.front: Domaine Vincent Dauvissat: in what year did the family first bottle its own Chablis?
cards.back: 1931, when bottling at the domaine was rare in Chablis.

cards.front: Which two grands crus does Dauvissat make, and which is the more open young?
cards.back: Les Clos and Les Preuses; Les Preuses is rounder and more open, Les Clos firmer and slower.

questions.q: A guest who knows only steel fermented Chablis asks what sets Dauvissat's Les Preuses apart. Which answer is right?
opts: It is raised in old oak casks and feuillettes
It is aged three years in new barriques
It is a premier cru from the left bank
It is a blend of several grand cru climats
questions.exp: Dauvissat raises its grands crus in oak, chiefly old barrels and feuillettes with little new wood; Les Preuses is a single grand cru climat on the right bank, not a premier cru or a blend.

questions.q: Dauvissat and Raveneau are named together as the Chablis domaines that raise grand cru in wood. What links them?
opts: Kinship by marriage and an old cask method
A single owner who bought both in 1989
Membership of the Chablis cooperative
A shared lease on the climat Les Preuses
questions.exp: The families are linked by marriage and both raise their grands crus in old casks; each is a separate family estate, and neither is a member of La Chablisienne, the cooperative.

report: The plan asks for Les Preuses or Les Clos: the library calls Les Clos the estate's most complete grand cru, but Les Preuses is kept, since Raveneau's record already teaches Les Clos, Les Preuses is the Dauvissat grand cru on the house's own list, and Decanter singles out the domaine's Les Preuses; no swap is proposed.

The founder (Robert Dauvissat in the accounts read) and his son are not named, for want of their dates in two sources; the grandson who took charge in 1989 is living and is not named outside the house's own name.
The accounts differ on when the son took over (1950 in one, through the 1950s in another), so the story says from the 1950s; the grandson's joining is 1976 in two accounts, told as the 1970s.
Organic farming since 2002 rests on Decanter and on an importer's page that says organic but not certified; the story says the early 2000s and claims no certificate.

The library's style line (old barrels, feuillettes, long lees ageing) carries the making; Decanter's note that the Preuses is wholly barrel aged with no taste of oak confirms it. Whether fermentation itself is in tank or barrel was not settled and is not said.
The sources give the aspect of Les Preuses as south, south west and south east, so the record gives its place on the hill and not its aspect.
The search budget shared by this run ran out before the domaine's own history could be read; the refuter should confirm 1931 and 1989 there if it can be reached.

changed: making and table: raised entirely and raised wholly in oak are now raised in oak, since some accounts give the grands crus months in tank after the barrel and before bottling.

label[2]: the claim that later labels read Vincent Dauvissat alone was not confirmed; the line now says the name many labels carry, for the founder's son and grandson, and that the domaine is also known by the grandson's name.
open: The years 1931 for the first bottling and 1989 for the grandson's taking charge rest on the author's searched secondary sources; the domaine's own history could not be read.

wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Bougros Côte Bouguerots
wine.classification: Grand Cru: a named parcel within Bougros, one of the seven climats of Chablis Grand Cru
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Côte Bouguerots, the steep part of Bougros, the climat at the north western end of the grand cru hill on the right bank of the Serein, on Kimmeridgian limestone and marl.
wine.making: Since the late 1990s the domaine has turned away from new oak: the grands crus are fermented and raised partly in steel tanks and partly in older oak barrels, kept on their lees and then bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Lemon curd, ripe pear and sea spray over chalk, broader and riper than most Chablis grand crus, with firm acidity, a supple middle and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Open within five years, it gains honey and hazelnut over the next ten and keeps longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air in the glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The one appellation shared by the seven climats on the hill across the Serein.
The climat at the north western end of the hill, one of the seven.
The steep parcel within Bougros: a named part of the climat, not an eighth grand cru.

records.table: Steep even by the measure of the Chablis hill, Côte Bouguerots is the part of Bougros that William Fèvre bottles under its own name. Raised since the late 1990s in steel and older oak, it is broad and ripe for Chablis, yet saline, and never tastes of wood.
records.story: When the law drew the Chablis appellations in 1938, it gave the seven climats of the hill above the Serein one name, Chablis Grand Cru, but the district it named was in decline: frost, phylloxera and war had left only a fraction of its old vineyard planted. The domaine was founded in 1959, on the eve of the district's recovery, and over the decades that followed its founder gathered parcels in Les Clos, Bougros, Les Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir until it held one of the largest shares of grand cru in the district. For years its wines were known for new oak, which divided opinion in a place that prizes the taste of its limestone. In 1998 the domaine was sold to the Henriot family of Champagne, who had bought Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune three years earlier, in 1995. The new owners turned the cellar away from new barrels and raised the grands crus partly in steel and partly in older oak. Côte Bouguerots is the steep part of Bougros, and the house bottles it under its own name, so that a guest can taste one slope within a climat. Here a large domaine's grand cru tastes of the hill, not of the cellar.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
others.note: From the domaine's largest grand cru holding, in the largest of the seven climats.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Preuses
others.note: A grand cru of rounder, more open character, from the north western reach of the hill.

traps: Côte Bouguerots is a named parcel inside Bougros, not an eighth grand cru: Chablis Grand Cru has seven climats.
A large holding is no sign of blending: Fèvre bottles each grand cru climat apart, and Côte Bouguerots apart within Bougros.
Heavy new oak marked the domaine's wines before 1998; since then it has raised its grands crus in steel and older barrels.

cards.front: William Fèvre: what is Côte Bouguerots, and is it an eighth grand cru?
cards.back: The steep part of the grand cru Bougros, bottled under its own name; a parcel within a climat, not an eighth grand cru.

cards.front: What changed at Domaine William Fèvre after its sale in 1998?

questions.q: A guest reads Bougros Côte Bouguerots on a William Fèvre label and asks what the second name means. What do you say?
opts: The steep part of the Bougros climat, bottled apart
An eighth grand cru added to Chablis in 1959
A premier cru that lies beside Bougros
A blend of Bougros with its neighbour Les Preuses
questions.exp: Côte Bouguerots is a named parcel within Bougros, one of the seven climats of Chablis Grand Cru; there is no eighth grand cru, and it is neither a premier cru nor a blend.

questions.q: In 1998 Domaine William Fèvre passed to new owners, three years after they had bought a Beaune house. Who were they?
opts: The Henriot family of Champagne
La Chablisienne, the growers' cooperative
The Moët Hennessy group of Épernay
The Rothschild family of Lafite
questions.exp: The Henriot family bought Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune in 1995 and Domaine William Fèvre in 1998; La Chablisienne is the Chablis cooperative of 1923.

report: The search budget shared by this run was spent before this house could be searched: the founding year, the holdings, the named parcel and the turn away from new oak are the library's; the sale of 1998 to the Henriot family and their purchase of Bouchard in 1995 rest on the author's reading of the Oxford Companion, not opened in this run, and on the Codex's own pairing of Bouchard Père et Fils with William Fèvre in the Court's list, and need the refuter's search.
The founder is not named: the author could not confirm whether he is living or find his dates.

The library calls Côte Bouguerots a parcel at the foot of the grand cru slope and the plan calls it the steep slope within Bougros; the record says only the steep part of Bougros, and the refuter should settle where on the slope it lies.
The library says Fèvre owns more grand cru than any other Chablis producer; that is a present holding, so the story says it gathered one of the largest shares, as history.
The present share of barrel and of any new wood was not confirmed, so the making says only partly steel and partly older oak since the late 1990s.

open: Where Côte Bouguerots lies on the slope: the library says at the foot of the grand cru slope, the plan the steep slope; the refuter reads it as the steep lower part of Bougros above the Serein, so the record keeps the steep part of Bougros.
Whether the founder is living was not settled, so he stays unnamed.

wine.name: Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru on the right bank of the Serein that carries the grand cru hill on to the south east beyond Blanchot, on Kimmeridgian limestone and marl.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in stainless steel tanks with no oak at any stage, as every wine of the domaine is, then left on its fine lees for many months before it is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon zest and wet chalk with a note of crushed shell, taut and pure with no trace of wood, high acidity and a long, saline finish; age brings honey and toasted hazelnut.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready after three or four years, it gains depth over ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of moderate size.

label.means: The tier between Chablis and Chablis Grand Cru, with the climat named after it.
The climat, beside the grand cru hill on the right bank of the Serein.
The name on the labels: Louis Michel and sons, the family domaine.

records.table: Not a stave of oak touches Louis Michel's Montée de Tonnerre: this Chablis premier cru from beside the grand cru hill is fermented and aged in steel alone. It is pure, taut and saline, with nothing between the fruit and the limestone, so pour it with oysters or white fish.
records.story: The domaine counts its beginnings from 1850, when Chablis was a busy vineyard sending its wine to Paris in cask, much of it in the small local barrel, the feuillette. The decades that followed were hard on it: phylloxera, two wars and the spring frosts left only a fraction of the old vineyard standing, and when the law drew its appellations in 1938 the district was at a low ebb. Recovery came after the 1960s, when sprinklers and heaters against frost let growers plant again, and through it the Michel family took the opposite road from the old barrel domaines. In the second half of the twentieth century they gave up oak altogether, and every wine of the house, grand cru included, has since been fermented and aged in stainless steel. Their argument is that Chablis needs nothing from wood: the cold climate and the Kimmeridgian marl give the acidity, the salt and the shell, and steel keeps them clear. Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru that carries on from the grand cru hill, is where that argument is heard at its fullest. Poured beside a Raveneau or a Dauvissat from the same ground, it shows a guest what the cellar changes and what the vineyard does not.

others.name: Chablis Premier Cru Montmains
others.note: A left bank premier cru from plots the family replanted in the 1980s, made in steel.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Grenouilles

cards.front: Where does Montée de Tonnerre lie, and what is its rank?
cards.back: On the right bank of the Serein, carrying the grand cru hill on beyond Blanchot; it is a premier cru.

questions.q: A guest wants a Chablis premier cru that has never touched wood. Why does Louis Michel's Montée de Tonnerre fit?
opts: The domaine ferments and ages every wine in steel
It is raised in old feuillettes that give no flavour
Chablis premier cru may not legally see oak
It is blended from several left bank climats

questions.q: Louis Michel took the opposite road from the old barrel domaines of Chablis. When did the family give up oak?
opts: In the second half of the twentieth century
When the domaine was founded in 1850
When the appellation was drawn in 1938
In the decade after phylloxera reached Chablis

wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Château Grenouilles
wine.classification: Grand Cru, from Grenouilles, one of the seven climats of Chablis Grand Cru
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: The vines of Château Grenouilles, which cover most of Grenouilles, the smallest of the seven climats, between Vaudésir and Valmur on the grand cru hill, on Kimmeridgian limestone and marl.
wine.making: Picked from the château's own vines and vinified apart from the cooperative's other wines, it is raised on its fine lees for many months before the cooperative bottles it under the château's name.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon peel and white blossom over chalk dust, with a cool sea breeze note, a supple, rounded middle and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Open after four or five years, it gains honey and hazelnut over ten and keeps longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate in Grenouilles whose vines the cooperative works; a cooperative's wine, not a private grower's.
The one appellation shared by the seven climats on the hill.
The Chablis growers' cooperative, founded in 1923, which makes and bottles the wine.

records.table: Château Grenouilles is La Chablisienne's grand cru, from most of Grenouilles, the smallest of the seven Chablis climats. It shows what a cooperative of growers can bottle at grand cru level: supple, saline and scented with white blossom, and ready sooner than the barrel domaines.
records.story: After the First World War Chablis was a shrunken vineyard: phylloxera had taken most of its vines, and its growers sold their grapes and wine to the merchants. In 1923 a group of them joined together to make and sell their wine as one, and La Chablisienne was born. Fifteen years later, in 1938, the law gave the seven climats of the grand cru hill a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. The cooperative grew with the district's recovery after the 1960s, when protection against spring frost let the vineyard spread again, until its members farmed a large share of the appellation. Grenouilles is the smallest of the seven climats, set between Vaudésir and Valmur; its name means frogs, which, the story goes, once sang from the banks of the Serein below. Most of it came to belong to Château Grenouilles, an estate whose vines the cooperative works and whose wine it bottles apart under the château's name. That a grand cru should come from a cooperative surprises many guests, and it is a question the Court asks. Château Grenouilles is the proof that Chablis Grand Cru is not the wine of small domaines alone.

Château Grenouilles is a cooperative wine, not a private grower's estate bottling.
Louis Michel also holds vines at the top of Grenouilles; Château Grenouilles is La Chablisienne's wine from most of the climat.

cards.front: What sets Grenouilles apart among the seven Chablis grand cru climats, and who bottles most of it?
cards.back: It is the smallest of the seven; La Chablisienne bottles most of it as Château Grenouilles.

questions.q: A guest orders La Chablisienne's grand cru and asks where it stands among the seven climats. What do you tell them?

It is the largest, beside Blanchot
It is a premier cru below the hill
It is a blend of all seven climats

questions.q: A guest is surprised that a Chablis grand cru comes from a cooperative. When did the growers of La Chablisienne first join together?
opts: In 1923, after the First World War
In 1938, with the appellation decree
In 1959, as frost protection spread

report: The search budget shared by this run ran out before the cooperative's own history page could be read; the founding year, Château Grenouilles from most of the climat and Grenouilles as the smallest climat are the library's, the place of Grenouilles on the hill and its soil are the Chablis wine bodies', and the rest on the author's reading of the Oxford Companion, not opened in this run.

The year the cooperative came to work the Château Grenouilles vines (2000 in the author's recollection) and the man who led the founding of 1923 (a priest of Chablis in the same recollection) are left out for want of a source.

The making, part oak barrel and part tank for about a year, is the author's account of the cooperative's grand cru practice and is unconfirmed: the refuter should check the cooperative's own sheet for Château Grenouilles.
The library says the cooperative draws on a large share of the appellation's planted area; the story keeps that as history of its growth, not a present figure.
The frogs of the name are told as a story.

changed: making: the split between oak barrel and tank and about a year on the lees, which the author marked unconfirmed and the refuter could not settle, are taken out; the wine is vinified apart and raised on its lees for many months.
open: The year the cooperative came to the Château Grenouilles vines (2000 in the author's recollection, 2003 in the refuter's) is left out.
The priest who led the founding of 1923 is left unnamed, his dates not found.
